title: Come with me if you want big forearms (7 Steps MASSterplan)
summary: A seven-step forearm plan in novice, intermediate and advanced stages, where moving up depends on grip stamina and training frequency rather than load. He rejects forearm black-pills and the idea that heavy pulls are enough, favours the arm-wrestler isolation route over the strongman route, and treats grip stamina as a currency to spend wisely.
claims: Most people know forearm lifts but fail to strategize; he applied this plan for 5-6 months with great results
Progress through the forearm plan is gated by stamina, volume capacity and how many days a week you can train forearms, not by load
Natural lifters with big forearms all share huge forearm stamina that let them train them a lot for a long time; lifters often have their best forearms in their 30s-40s
Forearms grow slowly because they are used constantly in daily life, like calves; patience is required and the intermediate stage can take years
Forearm genetics black-pills (insertions, small wrists) stop progress; he has very small wrists and skinny forearms and still grew them
Heavy deadlifts, rows and pull-ups alone do not build big forearms for most lifters; only gifted outliers grow that way, so isolate
Take advice from people who struggled to grow, not from genetic outliers for whom everything works
Grip training (closing the hand and holding heavy things) is an isometric contraction training only one forearm function; it is not enough for maximal forearm hypertrophy
Treat grip stamina as a currency to exchange for forearm development; do not spend it all on isometric holds
Strongman forearms come from huge bodyweight and whole-body stress; follow the arm-wrestler route instead: lighter athletes with 15-16 inch forearms trained by pure isolation without systemic fatigue
Train flexion, extension, pronation, supination and elbow flexion in addition to some isometric work
Step 1 (novice): pick one forearm isolation movement based on enjoyment, not optimality; treat it like picking a toy
For novices forearm isolation is optional; most early forearm growth comes from gripping during pulls, and pulls for the upper back take priority
Step 2 (novice): 3-4 sets per week max of 6-12 reps, done on days grip is not needed for pulls or after pulls
Hammer curls chosen as a biceps movement in the arm plan count as the novice forearm movement
For all forearm movements stay between 6 and 15 reps: below 6 grip becomes limiting, above 15 the pump comes too fast and reduces forearm recruitment, as rock climbers know
Go to forearm failure, not grip failure; arm wrestlers do hundreds of sets weekly without failure but we have little room so we maximize each set
You graduate the novice stage when grip limits your upper back work, e.g. you can no longer deadlift heavy without straps or mixed grip
Use straps where grip is the limiting factor to save grip stamina for forearm isolation; he does not use straps for pull-ups or dumbbell rows because grip does not limit him
Step 3 (intermediate): add 1-2 new forearm movements, either new wrist/elbow motions or pulls modified so the forearm is the limiting factor (fat grip pull-ups, towel curls, fat-grip hammer curls)
Step 4: 6-12 weekly sets of forearm work including grip work, with isolation (flexion, extension, pronation, supination) always prioritized over grip work

Only take isometric grip work to failure if you have no more forearm work that day or it will not impair recovery; failing on forearm isolation is easier to recover from than failure where the hand is pried open
Step 5 (intermediate): nucleus overload makes the most sense for forearms out of all muscles
Dead hangs at the end of every lower session are the best isometric forearm work and good for spine and shoulder; do not always go to failure
Use finger-extension bands to open the hand and prevent elbow and wrist issues from heavy gripping; also helps carpal tunnel
You clear the intermediate stage when 12 sets stop working, you cannot add load, or forearms recover faster than you can tax them
Step 6 (advanced): add 2-3 more movements to cover every wrist and elbow function and rotate; some biceps isolation can be swapped for hybrid lifts
For forearm isolation on the preacher bench, have the weight sit atop the wrist, never under it
Step 7 (advanced): no weekly set cap; hit forearms at every opportunity, with grip stamina management and frequency as keys
He is personally at step 5 of the plan
exercises: counts as forearm movement; fat grips make forearm the limit

best isometric forearm work, good for spine and shoulders
